I am seventy this year, and I have been working these flat fields in Quzhou County since I was a boy. The season is just starting, and my winter wheat is already in the ground from last October—about six and a half mu of it. I will see that through to harvest in June, then follow immediately with summer maize on the same land. Wheat and maize are the only crops I trust at my age; the grain station always buys them, and I do not have the strength to bend over cotton rows all summer or gamble on vegetable prices. For the wheat, I will spread a top-dressing of urea at green-up, irrigate three more times—winter water, jointing, and grain filling—and spray herbicide once and insecticide once or twice for weeds and aphids. I hire the rotary tiller for wheat preparation, but after the June harvest I will sow the maize with the no-till seeder to save my back. I will plant a hybrid like Denghai 605, put down compound fertilizer at sowing, irrigate twice if the summer turns dry, and spray for weeds and corn borers a couple of times. That is my plan for the year; it is steady, and it will not kill an old man.
